questions.question: What does treating 'rotation as a vector transformation' allow you to do?
options: Nothing useful for dice reasoning
Mathematically compute how face directions change after a rotation, rather than visualizing it purely by intuition
Only applies to 2D shapes, not cubes
Eliminates the need to know any cube facts
questions.rationale: Modeling rotation as a vector transformation lets you compute the resulting face directions precisely, rather than relying purely on mental visualization.

questions.question: What is described as 'the most important exam pattern' in dice reasoning?
options: A single view of a die with no further information
Being given three different views of the same die and having to deduce hidden face relationships from them
A die with no numbers on it
A question with no valid answer
questions.rationale: The classic and most common exam pattern presents three different views of the same die, requiring the solver to cross-reference them to deduce hidden relationships.

questions.question: What does an 'adjacent-face table' organize?
options: A list of die colors
A reference listing which faces are adjacent to each given face, based on the views provided
The die's manufacturing details
A random list of numbers
questions.rationale: An adjacent-face table systematically organizes which faces are known to be adjacent to each face, built up from the information given across multiple views.

questions.question: What is the 'opposite-face table method' used for?
options: Listing every face's color
Systematically tracking and deducing which face is opposite each other face, based on cross-referencing multiple views
Measuring the cube's dimensions
Randomly assigning opposite pairs
questions.rationale: This method builds a systematic table cross-referencing multiple views to deduce and track which faces are opposite which, rather than guessing.

questions.question: What does the 'common face rule' state when comparing two views of a die?
options: Two views can never share a common face
If two views share exactly one common face shown in the same position/orientation, that shared face can be used to align and compare the rest of the two views
Shared faces always indicate an invalid pair of views
Common faces are irrelevant to solving the problem
questions.rationale: A shared face in the same position across two views acts as an anchor, letting you align and directly compare the remaining faces of both views.

questions.question: Why is the 'same two faces — detailed explanation' section likely important?
options: Because sharing two faces provides no extra information
Because two views sharing two common faces provide a much stronger constraint for determining the third (differing) faces' relationship than sharing only one
Because two shared faces always means the views are invalid
Because it only applies to symbol dice
questions.rationale: Sharing two common faces between views is a much stronger constraint than sharing just one, since it more tightly pins down the possible relationship of the remaining differing face.

questions.question: Why is 'one face common' between two views generally NOT enough to draw a firm conclusion?
options: It is always enough on its own
Because a single shared face doesn't fully fix the relative orientation of the other faces, leaving multiple possible arrangements consistent with it
Because a single shared face is always an error
Because standard dice never share exactly one face between views
questions.rationale: A single shared face still leaves the die free to be rotated around that face, meaning several different arrangements of the remaining faces remain consistent with it.

questions.question: What does the rule 'opposite face cannot be adjacent' allow you to immediately rule out?
options: Nothing, this rule has no practical use
Any proposed answer or arrangement that shows two known-opposite faces as touching or adjacent, since that's geometrically impossible
Any answer with an even-numbered face
Only answers involving symbol dice
questions.rationale: This rule provides an instant elimination check: any candidate answer showing two known-opposite faces as adjacent can be immediately ruled out as geometrically impossible.

questions.question: What is the 'hidden face principle'?
options: That dice have no hidden faces
In any single view of a die, exactly three faces are hidden (not visible), and reasoning must account for what can and cannot be deduced about them
That all six faces are always visible at once
That hidden faces are irrelevant to solving any problem
questions.rationale: Since only 3 of a cube's 6 faces are visible in any single view, the other 3 are hidden — the hidden face principle is about correctly reasoning about what can (and can't) be concluded about them.

questions.question: In a single view showing 3 faces of a standard cube, how many faces remain hidden?
questions.rationale: 6 total faces minus the 3 visible faces leaves exactly 3 hidden faces.
